notes.meaning: Job paused to see if Zophar would take his turn to speak, but the three friends remained completely silent. Their silence showed they had run out of arguments against him. Job then resumed speaking with a grave, weighty message, teaching with authority like a proverb.

Job takes a solemn oath by the living God, which was the highest possible vow. He feels deeply wounded because God has not yet stepped in to clear his name or grant him a fair hearing. Even while complaining of his bitter pain, he still entrusts his life to God as the true Judge.

Job remembers that God breathed the breath of life into man, and that same breath still keeps him thinking clearly. As long as he lives, he refuses to say anything false or pretend to be someone he is not. Confessing to secret sins he did not commit would be a lie against God and his own conscience.

Job completely rejects the idea of agreeing with his friends' harsh accusations. He insists he will never claim they are right just to end the dispute. Until his dying breath, he will hold firmly to his genuine devotion and integrity before God.

Job refuses to let go of his upright character or admit that his troubles were caused by hidden crimes. Conscience is the inner awareness that tells us if we have done right or wrong, and Job's heart does not condemn his past life. He knows he is not sinless, but he has lived with a clear conscience before God.

Job states that anyone who falsely accuses him acts like a wicked opponent. In biblical law, a malicious accuser was meant to receive the very punishment he tried to bring on the innocent. Job makes it clear that true wickedness belongs to those who slander him, not to his own life.

Job asks what real hope an ungodly hypocrite has when his earthly life is taken away. A person might cheat others and gather great riches in this world, but those gains cannot save his soul. When God summons him to judgment, all of his worldly hope completely vanishes.

When sudden disaster strikes an ungodly person, God will not listen to his panicked cries. Someone who ignored God during times of ease and kept on sinning cannot expect divine favor at the last minute. Because his heart never truly turned to God, his prayers in distress are useless.

A hypocrite takes delight in worldly pleasures and money rather than in the Almighty. He may go through religious routines when things are comfortable, but he abandons prayer when hard times come. Job points to his own continuous prayers as clear proof that he is not a fake believer.

Job offers to instruct his friends about the great power and true dealings of God. He will not speak from mere human guesswork, but by the directing hand of the Almighty. He promises to explain the real principles behind how God rules the world.

Job reminds his companions that they have seen God's ways with their own eyes. Since they have witnessed life as it truly is, their accusations against him are totally baseless. They make a foolish mistake when they claim that every suffering person must be under God's wrath.

Job begins to describe the ultimate fate of cruel and wicked oppressors. Even though such ruthless people may flourish for a time, ruin is their true heritage from the Almighty. Job agrees that God finally punishes the wicked, but he denies that this pattern applies to his own pain.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars consider verses 13–23 to be Zophar's missing third speech that was accidentally placed under Job's name, because its description of the wicked matches the friends' arguments.

notes.meaning: A wicked man may have a very large family, which was often viewed as a special blessing. Yet his many children are destined to fall in battle or suffer from starvation. Earthly power cannot protect a sinner's descendants from the reach of divine justice.

Any family members who survive war and famine will be swept away by deadly plagues. Their deaths will be so sudden and shameful that they will not receive an honorable burial. Even their widows will not weep, either overwhelmed by grief or relieved that a tyrant is gone.

A greedy oppressor may pile up silver like dirt and gather great mounds of fine clothing. Yet he will not enjoy what he took from others. God's quiet providence will eventually place those fine garments on the righteous and divide the hoarded wealth among the innocent.

The house a wicked person builds looks grand, but it is as fragile as a moth's cocoon. It is like the temporary shelter a watchman sets up in a vineyard for the harvest season. As soon as the season passes or rough weather hits, it easily collapses and disappears.

The wealthy man goes to sleep thinking his fortune is completely safe, but he will never do so again. In an instant, sudden death strikes him in the night. When morning comes, he opens his eyes into eternity and all his earthly possessions are gone.

Dreadful terrors rush over the wicked person like an unstoppable flood. Judgment seizes him unexpectedly, like a violent nighttime storm carrying away a tent. He finds himself powerless against the sudden wave of God's displeasure.

A fierce east wind picks up the wicked man and sweeps him away from his home. In the ancient desert, this burning wind brought ruin and destroyed whatever stood in its path. In the same way, God's judgment blasts the ungodly and clears them out of their place.

God hurls His judgments against the guilty man without showing any pity. The sinner tries desperately to run and hide, but no one can escape the Almighty's hand. Those who refuse to seek God's mercy will find nowhere to run when judgment falls.

People clap their hands and hiss in scorn as the wicked tyrant is driven out of society. In ancient times, clapping and hissing were gestures used to chase a disgraced leader away in shame. Instead of being remembered with honor, his name is left with lasting disgrace.
